content: Rifampin may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as urine screenings for opiates or blood serum folate/vitamin B12 levels, potentially leading to false test results. Additionally, it can make it more difficult for the body to eliminate specific chemicals used in gallbladder tests. In the event of an overdose, if the individual exhibits severe symptoms such as loss of consciousness or difficulty breathing, immediately call emergency services (911). Otherwise, contact a poison control center without delay. In the United States, you can reach the poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. Before starting this medication and during its use, laboratory and medical tests (e.g., liver and kidney function tests, bilirubin levels, and complete blood counts) may be conducted to monitor your condition and response to treatment. It is essential to attend all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments. This medication has been prescribed specifically for your current condition. Do not use it for other conditions unless directed by your doctor. If you miss a dose, it is crucial to take the medication as scheduled. Contact your doctor or pharmacist promptly to establish a new dosing schedule. For storage, refer to the product instructions or consult your pharmacist for specific details. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless explicitly instructed to do so. Properly dispose of this product when it is expired or no longer needed. This information was last revised in May 2024. It is a summary and does not include all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that the product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. This information is not a substitute for personalized medical advice. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. Rifampin is used to prevent and treat tuberculosis and other bacterial infections. It belongs to a class of drugs known as rifamycin antibiotics. This antibiotic is effective only against bacterial infections and will not work for viral infections, such as the common cold or flu. This medication is administered by injection into a vein as directed by your doctor, typically once or twice daily. If you are using this medication at home, ensure you learn all preparation and usage instructions from your healthcare professional. Before use, visually inspect the product for particles or discoloration. Do not use the liquid if either is present. It is critical to continue using this medication (and any other medications prescribed for tuberculosis) exactly as directed by your doctor. For optimal effectiveness, use this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. Complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Common side effects may include upset stomach, heartburn, nausea, or headache. This medication may also cause discoloration of urine, sweat, saliva, or tears (yellow, orange, red, or brown). This effect is harmless and will resolve once the medication is discontinued. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. However, rifampin may rarely cause serious, potentially fatal liver disease. It may also rarely lead to a severe intestinal condition caused by the bacteria Clostridium difficile (C. difficile), which can occur during treatment or weeks to months after treatment has stopped. Additionally, it may sometimes cause oral thrush or a new yeast infection. A very serious allergic reaction to this drug is rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the United States, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice about side effects. Before using rifampin, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other rifamycins (such as rifabutin), or any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that can cause allergic reactions or other problems. Alcohol consumption may increase the risk of liver disease. Rifampin may reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines (e.g., typhoid vaccine). During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly needed. If used during the last few weeks of pregnancy, it may increase the risk of bleeding in both the mother and infant. Notify your doctor immediately if you observe any bleeding in your newborn. Rifampin passes into breast milk but is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase your risk for serious side effects. This document does not include all possible drug interactions. Maintain a list of all the products you use (including prescription/nonprescription drugs and herbal products) and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Rifampin interacts with many medications and can accelerate the removal of other drugs from your body, potentially affecting their efficacy. This medication may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal birth control methods, such as pills, patches, or rings, which could result in pregnancy. Discuss with your doctor or pharmacist whether you should use reliable backup birth control methods while taking this medication.
